title: Rosalind and the Lantern
premise: During the year of the great storms, widowed lighthouse keeper Orsen Amberdale survives by keeping his head down—until the army requisitions the coastal town of Saltmere and its ledger of names, the only record of who lived, who drowned, and who was smuggled to safety by the resistance Rosalind, his late wife's sister, secretly led. When the occupying victors begin burning 'disloyal' entries, Orsen must copy the ledger and get the truth on the record before the victors' historians write Saltmere's survivors out of existence. Hunted through the storm season, he and Rosalind race the requisition officers to a hidden second ledger kept in the lighthouse lantern room itself, and Orsen must choose between the anonymity that kept him alive and the testimony that keeps the dead alive. In the end he testifies at the inquiry under his own name, the ledger survives, and Rosalind—once a ghost in his household—becomes the town's recorded keeper of its history.
about_author: Mara Marchetti is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing requisition records from occupied coastal towns. She writes historical fiction about the paper trails ordinary people leave behind.

chapters.title: The Year of the Great Storms
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A quiet autumn in Saltmere: Orsen trims the wicks, mends nets, and avoids the harbor gossip about the war turning. His only visitor is Rosalind, his late wife's sister, who brings bread and asks careful questions. Beat: the comfort—and cost—of invisibility.

chapters.title: Names in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The town clerk asks Orsen to help copy the parish ledger, and he sees every name: the drowned, the smuggled, the hidden. Rosalind lingers over certain entries. Beat: the dawning sense that paper holds more danger than the sea.

chapters.title: Grey Coats at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The army requisitions Saltmere; soldiers billet in homes, and a captain named Veyra demands the ledger 'for administrative review.' Rosalind, who ran the escape routes, realizes her network's names are all in it. Beat: fear arriving in clean uniforms.

chapters.title: The Widow's Bread
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen hides Rosalind in the lighthouse cellar as officers search houses. He lies for the first time in his life, badly, to Captain Veyra. Beat: invisibility ends the moment you lie for someone.

chapters.title: What the Sea Gave Back
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A storm washes up a drowned courier carrying a coded note addressed to 'R.' Orsen must decide whether to give it to her or burn it. He gives it. Beat: grief and loyalty pulling against self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Captain's History
chapters.summary: Veyra's POV. Veyra, a former academic turned requisition officer, begins drafting the official history of Saltmere, cross-checking the ledger against informants. She is not cruel—she is thorough, which is worse. Beat: the enemy as a mirror of the hero.

chapters.title: Entries Struck Through
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen sees the ledger returned with names struck through—marked 'unreliable'—including people he knows were saved by Rosalind's network. Beat: quiet horror; history being edited in real time.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Confession
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind admits to Orsen what his late wife knew and hid: the escape routes, the money, the names. She asks him to help copy the true ledger before Veyra's historians finish. Beat: the weight of a sister's secret finally shared.

chapters.title: Ink by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Nights of copying in the lantern room while the beam turns above; Rosalind dictates, Orsen writes, and old tenderness between them turns into partnership. Beat: love rekindling as an act of defiance.

chapters.title: The Informant
chapters.summary: Veyra's POV. An informant reports light burning in the lighthouse after hours. Veyra suspects smuggling of goods; she is close to guessing it is smuggling of truth. Beat: the net tightening.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The worst storm of the year approaches; the army orders the lighthouse dark to prevent signaling. Orsen must keep the light burning anyway—ships will break on the rocks otherwise. Beat: duty to the living versus obedience to power.

chapters.title: The Light That Would Not Go Out
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind mans the lamp while soldiers hammer at the door; Orsen holds the stair. The light stays lit; three fishing boats come home. Beat: open defiance, the town's first act of collective courage.

chapters.title: Arrest at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen is arrested for 'obstruction of requisition'; the copied ledger pages are nearly found, hidden in the oil store. Rosalind moves them in the chaos. Beat: sacrifice, and the terrible helplessness of the one left outside.

chapters.title: The Cell and the Question
chapters.summary: Veyra's POV. Veyra interrogates Orsen, not with threats but with questions: why should the record favor the losing side? Orsen answers with the names of the drowned. Beat: the moral argument of the novel stated plainly.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Carried
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind reveals the second, older ledger—her own—hidden in the lighthouse since the war's start, and the network of townsfolk willing to testify. Beat: from hiding to organizing; hope with a plan.

chapters.title: The Inquiry Is Announced
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A victors' inquiry into 'civilian conduct' comes to Saltmere; testimony will be taken from the ledger, not the living. Orsen is released as a minor case to keep the peace. Beat: the race now has a finish line.

chapters.title: Every Name Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind organizes the town: each family with a struck-through name will stand at the inquiry and say it aloud. Orsen will present the true ledger. Beat: the town reclaiming its own history.

chapters.title: Veyra's Choice
chapters.summary: Veyra's POV. Veyra discovers the second ledger and, alone in the requisition office, must decide whether to burn it or let it be entered into the record. Her own historian's conscience turns. Beat: the antagonist's crisis; the price of survival weighed against the price of a lie.

chapters.title: The Hearing at Saltmere
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The inquiry: Veyra enters both ledgers into the record, struck names read aloud by the town, Orsen testifying under his full name for the first time in years. Beat: climax—truth on the record at last.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: Veyra's POV. Veyra is recalled in disgrace; Rosalind is briefly detained and released when the town vouches for her en masse. The ledgers are sealed as evidence—and thus preserved. Beat: victory that is partial, real, and costly.

chapters.title: The Keeper of the Record
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Spring: the army withdraws, the town rebuilds, and Rosalind is appointed keeper of the restored parish record. She and Orsen, quietly, begin a life together. Beat: inheritance redefined—not property, but memory.

chapters.title: Rosalind and the Lantern
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Years later, Orsen watches Rosalind light the lantern and read names to a new generation each storm-season eve. The final ledger entry is their own: two names, one light. Beat: resolution—love, duty, and truth reconciled in a single flame.
